facts.fact_text: The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the City of Sunderland College's proposal to build on the Arena.

The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to persuade the Council not to grant the City of Sunderland College permission to build on the Arena.
On or around 14 March 1998, the first applicant, together with her husband and son, set up two stands at the entrance of the shopping mall in the Galleries.
The stands set up by the first applicant on or around 14 March 1998 displayed posters alerting the public to the likely loss of the open space known as the Arena.
The stands set up by the first applicant on or around 14 March 1998 were used to seek signatures to present to the Council on behalf of Washington First Forum.
The fourth applicant continued to try to reach the public by setting up stands by the roadside on public footpaths.
The fourth applicant continued to try to reach the public by going to the old town centre at Concord.
Security guards employed by Postel Properties Limited would not let the first applicant or her assistants continue to collect signatures on any land or premises owned by Postel Properties Limited.
The applicants had to remove their stands from the Galleries.
The applicants had to stop collecting signatures at the Galleries.
In his reply of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries refused the third applicant access to the Galleries and adjacent car parks.
In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that the Galleries is unique in that although it is the Town Centre, it is also privately owned.

In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that the owner's stance on all political and religious issues is one of strict neutrality and that he was charged with applying this philosophy.

In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that he was obliged to refuse permission for Washington First Forum to carry out a petition within the Galleries or the adjacent car parks.
The third applicant's letter of 19 April 1998 to the manager of the Galleries remained unanswered.
At common law, a private property owner may in certain circumstances be presumed to have extended an implied invitation to members of the public to come onto his land for lawful purposes.
At common law, the implied invitation to members of the public to enter private property applies to commercial premises such as shops, theatres and restaurants.
At common law, there is a presumption that a house owner authorises people to come up the path to his front door to deliver letters or newspapers or for political canvassing.
At common law, any implied invitation to members of the public to enter private property may be revoked at will.
At common law, a private person's ability to eject people from his land is generally unfettered and he does not have to justify his conduct or comply with any test of reasonableness.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), the Court of Appeal held that CIN Properties Ltd had the right to determine any licence which the applicants might have had to enter the shopping centre in Wellingborough.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips allowed the appeal on the basis that CIN Properties Ltd had the right, subject only to the issue under section 20 of the Race Relations Act 1976, to determine any licence the applicants may have had to enter the shopping centre.

The Galleries is located within an area owned by Postel Properties Limited ('Postel'), a private company.
The Galleries, as owned by Postel Properties Limited at the relevant time, comprised a shopping mall with two hypermarkets and major shops.
The Galleries, as owned by Postel Properties Limited at the relevant time, comprised surrounding car parks with spaces for approximately 3,000 cars.
The Galleries, as owned by Postel Properties Limited at the relevant time, comprised walkways.
Public services were available in the vicinity of the Galleries.

From 31 January to 6 March 2001, Sunderland Council ran a consultation campaign under the banner 'Your Council, Your Choice'.
The 'Your Council, Your Choice' campaign informed local residents of three leadership choices for the future of Sunderland Council.
Sunderland Council was allowed to use the Galleries for the 'Your Council, Your Choice' consultation campaign.
The 'Your Council, Your Choice' campaign was a statutory consultation exercise carried out under section 25 of the Local Government Act 2000.
